7.text: In one tale, a woman deserted by her husband is left with five children.

8.text: She supports them with great difficulty, gathering edible roots for food.

9.text: Wandering in the desert, she comes to a dwelling on the seashore. A woman

10.text: sits at the entrance. The man returns from a sea-hunt, dragging a seal.

11.text: The deserted wife recognizes her husband. She resolves to avenge herself,

12.text: waits until the man leaves again, and then enters the house, makes friends

13.text: with the woman, and perfidiously kills her while she is asleep. Then she

14.text: returns to her own house. Her husband comes back, and, finding the woman

15.text: dead, guesses that it is the work of his first wife. He grabs his spear, goes

16.text: to the first wife. He arrives. She is not at home. She is wandering again

17.text: in the desert. The children cry, “Father, father has come!” — “Where did

18.text: your mother go?” — “Along that road. We shall follow her.” — “No, no!

20.text: roots. “I have found her; now I will kill her!” He cries, “I will kill you.”

21.text: She fled along the river. He overtook her. “Are you not my husband?

22.text: Why do you want to kill me? I have little children.” — “Why did you

23.text: mock me?” He aimed at her with his spear. She seized the spear, broke

24.text: it to pieces. Drawing her cowl over her head, she became a she-bear. She

25.text: squeezed the husband. “Oh, I pray you, let go! Come home! I shall always

26.text: work and bring meat.” She only growled and squeezed him to death.²

29.text: Group-Marriage. — Marriage among the Chukchee does not deal with

30.text: one couple only, but extends over an entire group. The Chukchee group-

32.text: to such a marriage-union are called “companions in wives” (ñew-tuˊmg̣ɪt).
